clean_story:
Instant reaction. Body’s alarm system.

The term fear response describes the automatic chain of events that prepares a body to face danger, like a car engine revving before a race. When eyes or ears detect a threat, the amygdala—a small almond-shaped part of the brain—sends an urgent signal. The adrenal glands then flood the bloodstream with adrenaline and cortisol, sharpening focus, speeding the heart, and tensing muscles. This is the fight-or-flight response, shared by humans and animals alike. A deer freezing at a rustling bush uses the same mechanism. In modern life, this system can misfire, triggering panic over non-threatening events like public speaking. Fear responses are not just reflexes; they are finely tuned by experience, like a musician adjusting an instrument after each note.
Three related subjects are stress hormones, animal survival instincts, and how memory shapes fear.
